extracted.intended_audience: students, thinkers, and legislators interested in political philosophy and statecraft
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts Aristotle's practical and normative prescriptions about household and city organisation — roles, property regimes, education, office rotation, and revenue-raising — intended to guide legislators and political theorists in designing well-ordered polities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of improving a fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three principal methods of making money by exchange: merchandise (carried on by sea or land or selling at source), usury, and receiving wages for work (either mean arts or bodily labour); and a third species between exchange and nature (produce from the earth, e.g., timber, metallurgy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle enumerates these as the main profitable pursuits; practical particulars are left to specialist authors. He gives examples (Thales' olive monopoly; a Sicilian who bought up iron) showing that contrivances like monopolies can be gainful but may be judged inconsistent with public affairs and restrained by rulers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and danger of monopoly for raising money
rubrics_metrics.description: To contrive a monopoly of any commodity is generally gainful; cities sometimes monopolise commodities to raise money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Thales hired oil-works cheaply and resold at will; a Sicilian bought up iron, made a profit, was then forbidden to remain. Useful for politicians to understand, but may be inconsistent with public affairs and therefore subject to prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three parts of domestic government
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three parts of domestic government: the masters, the fathers, and the husbands; the government of wife and children should both be that of free persons, but not the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific rule: the wife should be treated as a citizen of a free state, the children should be under kingly power (father's authority is founded in affection and seniority). The distinctions of form, expression, and honours should mark who governs and who is governed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise virtues of household members over possessions
rubrics_metrics.description: Greater attention should be paid to the several members of a family and their virtues than to the possessions or riches of it; greater attention to freemen than to slaves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle argues the moral character of household members is more important for the good of the family/state than wealth. This informs decisions on education and governance within the household.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue must be suited to station
rubrics_metrics.description: All persons ought to possess moral virtue, but the virtues differ in kind according to natural governing/submitting principles; the one who is to govern ought to be perfect in moral virtue, others need only that portion suited to their station.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle distinguishes the virtues of rulers and ruled (e.g., a man's courage consists in commanding, a woman's in obeying). Slaves lack power of determination and should be trained to virtues appropriate to their role by their masters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slaves and artisans: instruction according to role
rubrics_metrics.description: Slaves ought to be trained to those virtues proper for their situation by their master; they are not to be deprived of reason, and need more instruction than children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle rejects views that slaves lack reason entirely; instead, their moral education should be oriented toward their practical use and station. Artificers nearer to slavery in function should have similar virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: A city must be one but not too one
rubrics_metrics.description: The members of every state must have some things in common, but a city contracted too much to unity ceases to be a city; diversity and multiplicity of sorts are necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete community (e.g., total common ownership of wives, children, property as in Plato's proposal) would reduce a city to a family or a single person and thus destroy the city. Unity should be cultivated but bounded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against full communal wives and children
rubrics_metrics.description: Community of wives and children is attended with many difficulties and cannot produce the proposed ends; it leads to neglect, uncertainty about filiation, weaker friendship, and increased quarrels and sexual improprieties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle gives concrete harms: carelessness about children when relation is diffused, risk of incestuous relations, more frequent blows, murders, quarrels, and legal complications. He argues familial bonds and friendship (which prevent sedition) are undermined by such communal arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property regime: private ownership with common use
rubrics_metrics.description: It is best to have property private, but to make the use of it common; this balances incentives and communal mutual aid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private property encourages industry, attention to one's own concerns, and enables virtues like liberality and modesty; in well-governed cities some things may function 'in a manner common' (e.g., Lacedaemonian practice of using each other's slaves, horses, provisions). How to bring citizens to share use is a legislator's task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against complete community of goods
rubrics_metrics.description: A community of property (everything common) is difficult and impracticable: it creates disputes, mismatch between labour and consumption, negligence, and quarrels even among small numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle argues experience (colony settlements, communal households) shows community of goods produces conflicts rather than concord; private appropriation with some shared uses is superior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education, manners, philosophy and laws cultivate unity
rubrics_metrics.description: The people ought to be made one by education, manners, philosophy, and laws rather than by total community of goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Lacedaemon and Crete used education and public tables to create unity. Legislators should use long-term experience and cultural formation rather than artificial communal property to foster concord.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office rotation and stability
rubrics_metrics.description: In free states governors and the governed alternately change place; where possible government continuing in the same hands is better, but where not possible rotation (by time or other regulation) ensures equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle notes that among freemen equality requires some alternation (annual terms or regulated turns); however, constant occupants of offices can create sedition, particularly among the courageous and warlike classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define social classes' roles and political participation
rubrics_metrics.description: A polity must clearly decide whether husbandmen and artisans have arms, share in governance, or are excluded; the legislator must state how non-military classes relate to the military and to governance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle critiques Socratic proposals that separate military guardians from husbandmen/artisans without clarifying their rights/responsibilities; failing to do so invites conflict and undermines the community of the military.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for the happiness of all citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislator ought to make all citizens happy; a state cannot be truly happy unless all or at least the greater part are happy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle rejects systems that render some classes (e.g., the military guardians) unhappy while claiming to make the city happy; happiness is not additive and must exist in every individual for the polity to claim collective happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislator must consider country and people; feasibility matters
rubrics_metrics.description: When framing laws a legislator should have two things in view: the country and the people; it must be possible to support proposed institutions given resources and population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle criticises impractical proposals (e.g., supporting thousands of idle guardians) and emphasises tailoring institutions to material conditions and the character of the populace.
